abstract: Co(III) polypyridyl complexes have emerged as promising first-row transition metal alternatives to noble-metal chromophores, yet their excited-state lifetimes and relaxation mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Here, we present computational strategies to predict excited-state lifetimes in the prototypical complex , integrating electronic structure theory, Marcus-type rate models, minimum-energy crossing point (MECP) analysis, and trajectory-based nonadiabatic dynamics simulations. Marcus theory is used to rationalize why Co(III) complexes operate in the inverted region, in contrast to isoelectronic Fe(II) systems, and explains how ligand-field tuning can simultaneously enhance redox power and prolong excited-state lifetimes. MECP-based transition-state theory yields nanosecond ground-state recovery times and reproduces the experimentally observed ligand-field trends across a series of substituted complexes. Beyond this static picture, surface hopping dynamics based on a parametrized linear vibronic coupling (LVC) Hamiltonian demonstrates that both sub-picosecond intersystem crossing and nanosecond triplet decay can be captured within a unified dynamical description. Analysis of nuclear motion reveals an impulsive Co–N bond elongation and coherent vibrational activity accompanying population transfer into the 3 MC manifold. We further derive practical guidelines for selecting the simulation time and number of trajectories in nonadiabatic dynamics studies targeting long-lived excited states. Together, these results establish a set of transferable computational strategies for predicting and rationalizing excited-state lifetimes in first-row transition metal complexes.

abstract: Natural products are a rich source of pharmacologically active scaffolds for anticancer drug discovery, and their integration with metal centres represents an attractive strategy for the development of novel metallodrugs. Gold(I) complexes are emerging as versatile anticancer agents, distinguished by their unique coordination chemistry and ability to modulate multiple cellular pathways. Incorporation of natural product scaffolds with gold(I) enhances biological activity, as these frameworks provide inherent recognition elements, redox activity, and structural complexity that synergistically complement the reactivity of the gold(I) centre. This review analyses natural product-conjugated gold(I) complexes, organised according to ligand classes, including terpenoids, phenolics, polyketides, and phenylpropanoids, with emphasis on coordination-driven structure-activity relationships. Beyond cytotoxic effects, recent studies discussed herein demonstrate their ability to suppress inflammation and trigger immunogenic cell death, supporting both direct and immune-mediated anticancer responses. Additionally, selected complexes exhibit imaging capabilities, illustrating how natural product scaffolds confer multifunctional therapeutic profiles. Building on these properties, emerging strategies are extending gold(I) chemistry into advanced biomedical applications, including enzyme-responsive delivery with peptide–gold conjugates, biomaterial integration in coumarin hydrogels, nucleic acid interactions using caffeine-derived ligands, drug repurposing through indomethacin-based gold complexes, and targeted radiochemotherapy via biotin-functionalised gold complexes. Collectively, these developments position natural product-gold(I) hybrids as versatile platforms with significant potential for next-generation cancer therapy.

abstract: The global shift toward sustainable energy and cleaner environments has intensified the demand for advanced catalytic systems for sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Integrating graphene and its derivatives with semiconductor photocatalysts has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance charge separation, improve light absorption, and increase the overall catalytic efficiency and durability. This review outlines the versatility of graphene and its derivatives, emphasizing the critical roles of surface chemistry and interface engineering, including surface functional groups and defect engineering, π-π interactions, adsorption mechanisms, charge transfer at graphene-catalyst interfaces, and surface wettability in governing their catalytic as well as environmental performance. Various synthesis strategies for graphene-based composites such as hydrothermal methods, in-situ growth, electrochemical deposition, microwave-assisted synthesis, and template-assisted approaches are summarized with key preparation parameters. Recent advances in graphene-derived composites, such as graphene-metal oxide, graphene-metal sulfide, graphene-metal-organic frameworks, and graphene two-dimensional material systems are discussed, which demonstrate significant potential for advanced electrocatalytic and photoelectrochemical water splitting applications. Their roles in environmental remediation are also examined, encompassing dye and phenolic degradation, adsorption-based heavy-metal removal, photocatalytic metal-ion reduction, and sensitive detection of heavy-metal species. Their quantized electronic states give rise to unique physicochemical properties. Significant progress has been made in synthesizing homometallic coinage metal NCs and their alloys, which exhibit notable photophysical and catalytic behaviors, serving as ideal models for investigating size-dependent growth processes at the atomic level. In contrast, NCs composed of non-noble metals are less explored because of their lower stability, which arises from vacant coordination sites, tendency toward oxidation, higher surface reactivity, and synthetic challenges. As a result, these systems more often form aggregated metal sulfide or metal oxide nanoparticles rather than atomically precise clusters. This review highlights advances in group-12 metal-based NCs–specifically zinc, cadmium, and mercury–including their homometallic forms, in which chalcogenide protected clusters have long been pursued as semiconductor materials as well as doped coinage metal alloys. Next, we discussed multidimensional cluster-assembled framework having group-12 clusters as a node. We summarize synthetic strategies, structural characterization, and structure-dependent optical properties of these compounds. The review concludes with a discussion on their potential applications in cutting-edge disciplines such as photonics, optoelectronics, bioimaging, sensing, and catalysis, and outlines potential future research directions.

abstract: Metal nanoclusters (NCs) composed of fewer than 200 atoms have emerged as novel catalysts due to their specific physicochemical properties and structural fluxionalities, which differ significantly from those of the corresponding bulk or nanoparticles. Among the various types of NCs, those composed of coinage metals (Au, Ag, Cu) have garnered particular interest due to their relatively simple electronic structures and the discovery of size-specific catalysis by Haruta and Hutchings. Given the substantial alterations in the fundamental properties of coinage-metal NCs that result from the addition or removal of even a single atom, it is imperative to synthesize them with atomic precision to establish the structure-catalysis relationship and to maximize their potential in catalysis. The protection by organic ligands, such as thiolates, phosphines, alkynyls, and N-heterocyclic carbenes, plays a pivotal role in the precise control of NC size, the enhancement of NC stability against aggregation, and the determination of their geometric structures through single-crystal X-ray diffractometry. However, the ligand-protected metal NCs typically exhibit poor catalysis, primarily due to the absence of active sites for chemical transformation. A growing body of research has demonstrated that the employment of designed ligands facilitates the circumvention of the trade-off between activity and durability in the catalytic application of ligand-protected metal NCs. The application of ligand engineering facilitates the modulation of the geometry, density, and electronic structure of active sites. Furthermore, it enables the characterization of key intermediates through a range of spectroscopic methodologies. This review article provides a synopsis of recent examples of ligand engineering, with the objective of gaining deeper insight into catalytic mechanisms on coinage-metal NCs. This article also discusses prospects and challenges for the development of superior metal NC catalysts.

abstract: Bimetallic metal–organic frameworks (BMOFs) have rapidly evolved into a powerful materials platform for next-generation supercapacitor (SC) electrodes by enabling atomic-level control, enhanced redox chemistry, tunable electronic structures, and pore architectures beyond the limits of monometallic frameworks. By co-incorporating two distinct metal centers within one crystalline lattice, BMOFs create synergistic metal–metal interactions that modulate d-band electronic states, generate flexible redox couples and promotes defect-rich coordination environments, collectively enhancing charge storage kinetics and active-site utilization. This review critically examines recent progress in BMOF design for SCs, emphasizing synthetic strategies that govern metal distribution, framework topology, hierarchical morphology, and compositional homogeneity. We discuss how dual-metal coordination and hierarchical porosity accelerate ion diffusion and charge transfer, while mitigating structural degradation during prolonged cycling. Particular attention is given to BMOF-based hybrid electrodes and BMOF-derived oxides, hydroxides, chalcogenides, and phosphides, where in situ framework conversion yields conductive, mechanically robust architectures with high pseudocapacitive activity. We further highlight how integration with advanced functional materials creates redox-active heterointerfaces that accelerate charge transfer, enhance active site utilization, and improve overall SC device performance. Finally, we highlight key bottlenecks including conductivity, scalability, and interfacial stability that must be addressed to translate BMOF-based materials into durable, high-energy SC devices.

abstract: Hierarchically porous metal-organic frameworks have emerged as a versatile platform for overcoming the mass transfer limitations of conventional microporous materials. However, the true potential of these materials lies not merely in increasing pore volume, but in the functional integration of distinct pore domains. Herein, we articulate the concept of pore-zoned nanoarchitectonics, a rational design paradigm that orchestrates reactants across varying length scales. We elucidate how this architecture creates a synergistic environment: micropores serve as confined redox centers for thermodynamic stabilization, mesopores act as kinetic buffers for intermediate management, and macropores function as high-flux reservoirs for phase boundary regulation. This review comprehensively summarizes state-of-the-art synthetic strategies—ranging from ligand engineering and defect formation to hard/soft templating and composite-derived approaches—that enable such precise structural programming. Furthermore, we highlight the transformative impact of these architectures in electrocatalysis, demonstrating how pore-zoned engineering resolves the intrinsic trade-off between mass transport velocity and active site density. Finally, we provide a roadmap for the future, emphasizing the transition from static porous solids to intelligent, adaptive energy conversion systems.

abstract: Phosphazides (R 3 P=N–N=N–R') are intermediates in the Staudinger reaction (R 3 P + N 3 –R' → R 3 P=N–R'), which is commonly employed to prepare iminophosphoranes/phosphinimines (R 3 P=N–R'). Phosphazides are rarely isolated due to their propensity to decompose via loss of dinitrogen (N 2 ), along with concomitant generation of a phosphinimine. While phosphinimines are commonplace in multidentate ligand frameworks, phosphazides have been largely overlooked as a viable functional group in coordination chemistry, despite their diverse coordination behavior. This review provides a comprehensive accounting of phosphazides coordinated to metal centres and describes their potential to stabilize metal complexes that exhibit novel reaction chemistry.

abstract: High-linear energy transfer (high-LET) radiation offers a promising strategy to overcome the limitations of conventional β − -emitters in resistant or heterogeneous tumors. This review highlights recent advances in high LET radiotheranostics from a coordination chemistry perspective, focusing on α-emitters ( 225 Ac, 227 Th, 212/213 Bi, and 212 Pb) and Auger electron-emitters ( 161 Tb, 64 Cu, and 191/193m/195m Pt). Therapeutic performance is governed by intrinsic metal ion properties, including ionic radius, charge density, and donor preference, which dictate complex stability, kinetic inertness, and resistance to recoil during decay. The large Ac 3+ ion requires high denticity chelators for efficient radiolabeling and in vivo stability, while recoil of daughter radionuclides ( 221 Fr, 213 Bi) remains a major redistribution challenge that has motivated nanoparticle and liposomal strategies. 227 Th forms stable complexes with 1-hydroxy-2(1H)-pyridinones (1,2-HOPO)-type ligands for antibody delivery, although bone-seeking 223 Ra generation must be considered. Short-lived 212 Bi/ 213 Bi and the 212 Pb/ 212 Bi in vivo generator system demand rapid labeling and appropriate pharmacokinetics, and ligands such as OCTAPA or DOTAM (TCMC) better match the coordination preferences of Bi(III) and Pb(II). Although 212 Pb enables element matched 203 Pb/ 212 Pb theranostics, daughter redistribution remains challenging. For Auger emitters, efficacy depends not only on complex stability but also on controlled intracellular localization. The coordination chemistry of Tb(III), Cu(II), and Pt(II) governs chelator selection and subcellular fate, as illustrated by [ 161 Tb]Tb-DOTA conjugates, stable 64 Cu complexes, and DNA targeting radioplatinum agents. Overall, this review establishes coordination-driven design principles for high-LET radiotheranostics, bridging inorganic chemistry and translational nuclear medicine toward next-generation precision radiotherapy.

abstract: The growing severity of climate change and rising energy demand for fossil fuels have increased interest in exploring clean energy and renewable sources. Electrochemical water splitting using renewable energy inputs has been considered the most promising approach to producing clean hydrogen (H 2 ). Water splitting involves oxygen evolution (OER) at the anode and hydrogen evolution reactions (HER) at the cathode. Common catalysts for OER and HER are composed of noble metals and non-metals, their alloys, and their compounds, but the high cost, scarcity, and stability of noble metals hinder wider application. To tackle this, cobalt-based complexes have been found to be homogeneous catalysts for both OER and HER, meeting the demand for low overpotentials. Cobalt complexes are highly promising, cost-effective electrocatalysts for electrochemical water splitting (EC-WS), and they can be precisely tuned both electronically and structurally in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), layered double hydroxides (LDHs), phosphides, chalcogenides, and single-atom catalysts (SACs). Selective tuning of their σ-donors, π-acceptors, and redox-active (non-innocent) ligands gives rise to different and measurable shifts of the cobalt d-band center, of e G orbital filling, and of the Co 2+ /Co 3+ /Co 4+ redox accessibility, respectively. This review explores the cobalt coordination environment, its donor/acceptor properties, its geometry, its oxidation state, and its nuclearity, and how these affect the three key HER/OER catalytic metrics: overpotential, Tafel slope, and turnover frequency (TOF). An inter-study comparison of various systems reveals that low-cost cobalt catalysts, in particular with optimized coordination environments: multinuclear cubane architectures and dual-site phosphide systems, are as competitive (or more) as IrO 2 and RuO 2 systems in alkaline OER (best ɳ 10 = 157 mV). We further critically assess the synthesis routes, degradation mechanisms (ligand dissociation, cobalt leaching, phase reconstruction), and homogeneous vs. heterogeneous aspects of cobalt catalysts under operating conditions of water splitting. The review ends with quantitative electronic descriptor targets and actionable strategies for scalable synthesis and commercially viable development.

title: First row transition metal dinuclear complexes for H2 production and CO2 reduction: from homogeneous to heterogeneous conditions
abstract: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO 2 RR) are key processes for the development of sustainable energy and carbon-neutral technologies. Molecular catalysts based on earth-abundant metals offer unique opportunities to address these challenges, owing to their well-defined structures and tunable reactivity. In particular, bio-inspired dimetallic complexes have emerged as powerful platforms for promoting HER and CO 2 RR through metal-metal cooperativity, as exemplified by natural hydrogenases and carbon monoxide dehydrogenases. This review summarizes recent advances in molecular HER and CO 2 RR electrocatalysis based on bio-inspired dimetallic complexes composed of 3d transition metals. We highlight how dinuclearity, functional differentiation between metal centers, and second-coordination-sphere effects enable reaction pathways inaccessible to mononuclear systems, leading to enhanced activity, lower overpotentials, and improved selectivity. Both homogeneous catalysts and immobilized molecular systems operating under electrochemical conditions are discussed, with immobilization considered as a strategy to stabilize molecular catalysts while preserving their intrinsic reactivity. Overall, this review provides design principles for developing efficient and sustainable molecular electrocatalysts for hydrogen production and CO 2 valorization.

Fifty years of coordination chemistry at the Laboratoire de Chimie de Coordination (LCC), Toulouse: diversity and impact
abstract: The “Laboratoire de Chimie de Coordination” (LCC) celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2024 in Toulouse, France. The LCC is a dedicated CNRS laboratory, created in 1974 under the impetus of the French Academician Fernand Gallais. Since then, the LCC has maintained a coherent and highly visible scientific orientation centered on the synthesis, reactivity, and applications of coordination chemistry and main-group chemistry. A first Special Issue of Coordination Chemistry Reviews was published on the occasion of the LCC's 40th anniversary.In this new Special Issue, prepared to celebrate the laboratory's 50th anniversary, members of the LCC research teams present reviews illustrating the remarkable diversity of coordination chemistry currently pursued at the LCC and its integration into the broader international research landscape. From fundamental research to applications, spanning catalysis (three reviews), materials science (four reviews), and biology and health sciences (four reviews), this Special Issue of Coordination Chemistry Reviews offers a comprehensive overview of the forefront of coordination and main-group chemistry, through contributions authored by researchers from across the LCC.

title: Rethinking MOFs for REE recovery: Role of functional groups, selectivity limitations, and possible future directions
Confinement-enhanced catalysis within nanoscale architectures: Bridging nanoreactors and synthetic organelles
Rational design of heterogeneous single-site catalysts via surface organometallic chemistry
abstract: Single-site heterogeneous catalysts offer an attractive route to unite the molecular precision of homogeneous catalysis with the durability and practical advantages of solids. Surface organometallic chemistry (SOMC) provides a particularly powerful strategy for this purpose by grafting molecular precursors onto tailored surfaces and converting support functionalities into ligand environments for isolated metal centers. As a result, SOMC brings the language and logic of coordination chemistry to heterogeneous catalysis, where the support becomes an integral part of the active site coordination sphere. This Review surveys recent progress in the rational design of SOMC-derived single-site catalysts, with emphasis on synthetic routes, post synthetic transformations, and the deliberate tuning of catalytic behavior through metal-support interactions. Discussions are made on how support identity, hydroxyl topology, acidity, and redox activity shape the geometry, electronic structure, and oxidation state of supported metal sites, as well as how these factors determine activity, selectivity, and stability. We also examine a central limitation of these systems: despite their molecularly informed design, supported single sites often exist as structurally distributed ensembles rather than uniform species, particularly on amorphous supports. This site heterogeneity, along with catalyst dynamics under operating conditions, remains a major barrier to definitive structure-activity relationships. Therefore, emerging approaches that combine advanced characterization, first-principles modeling, ensemble kinetics, and machine learning to resolve active-site structure and guide catalyst development are highlighted. Together, these advances position SOMC as a versatile coordination chemistry framework for the predictive design of heterogeneous catalysts with well-defined molecularly tailored active sites.

title: Edible metal-organic frameworks: coordination chemistry, design principles, and delivery functions
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are highly tunable coordination materials that have been widely investigated for adsorption, catalysis, and drug delivery. More recently, interest has emerged in frameworks constructed from biocompatible or food-relevant components, giving rise to the concept of “edible” MOFs for ingestion-related applications. However, this concept remains poorly defined, and the links between coordination chemistry, framework stability, and behavior under gastrointestinal conditions are not yet well established. This review critically examines MOFs built from food-compatible metals and ligands, with emphasis on how metal-ligand coordination, framework topology, and defect chemistry govern their structural stability, host-guest interactions, and release behavior. Cyclodextrin-based MOFs currently dominate the field and demonstrate improved loading, stabilization, and controlled release of hydrophobic or labile bioactives. Beyond these systems, frameworks based on organic acids, amino acids, and other biomolecules highlight a broader but largely underexplored design space of ingestible coordination materials. Across these systems, performance is closely linked to coordination features such as bond strength, aqueous stability, and framework degradation pathways. Despite promising functional properties, significant challenges remain in achieving predictable gastrointestinal release, scalable and food-compatible synthesis, and clear safety and regulatory profiles. Overall, edible MOFs represent an emerging subclass of coordination materials in which molecular-level design must be directly aligned with application constraints, offering new opportunities for integrating framework chemistry with complex delivery functions.

One ring to bind them all? A review on speciation, structure, kinetics, and radiochemistry of DOTA complexes formed with medically relevant radiometals
abstract: Radiopharmaceuticals have become an increasingly important modality for both the diagnosis and treatment of numerous diseases, particularly cancer. Their active moiety is usually a radioactive metal ion, bound to a tumor-targeting molecule via a chelating agent. Among the plethora of chelators developed for this purpose, 1,4,7,10-tetraazacyclododecane-1,4,7,10-tetraacetic acid (DOTA) is undoubtedly one of the most widely employed. This review examines selected properties of metal-DOTA complexes that are relevant to radiopharmaceutical applications. The discussion focuses on elements that have radioisotopes of current, past, or potential future clinical relevance: actinium, antimony, barium, bismuth, cerium, cobalt, copper, erbium, gallium, gold, holmium, indium, iridium, lanthanum, lead, lutetium, manganese, mercury, niobium, osmium, palladium, platinum, radium, rhenium, rhodium, rubidium, ruthenium, samarium, scandium, silver, strontium, tantalum, technetium, terbium, thallium, thorium, titanium, uranium, yttrium, and zirconium. The properties considered include: ( i ) speciation in aqueous solution (number, stoichiometry, and stability constants of metal-DOTA complexes); ( ii ) structure of the complexes; and ( iii ) kinetics of complex formation and dissociation. These data have been collected in a “DOTA Periodic Table of Elements of Radiopharmaceutical Interest”, which provides a compact graphical overview of the available information. In addition, the review summarizes radiochemical properties of metal-DOTA complexes, including radiolabeling yields and stability in biological environments. Despite the substantial body of literature on metal-DOTA complexes, this analysis reveals that important gap remains. For several elements, thermodynamics, structural or kinetic parameters are still unavailable, while in other cases reported data show significant variability and warrant critical re-evaluation.

Single-ion conducting polymer electrolytes: Molecular design strategies for high cation transference and ionic conductivity
abstract: Single-ion conducting polymer electrolytes (SICPEs) have emerged as promising solid-state electrolytes for next-generation rechargeable batteries, offering high ion transference number and improved safety compared to conventional dual-ion systems. However, achieving simultaneous high ionic transfer number and ion conductivity remains a critical challenge due to the inherent trade-off between anion immobilization and polymer chain mobility. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of molecular and structural design strategies aimed at decoupling Li + transport from bulk polymer segmental motion. Key approaches include backbone engineering, crosslinked network architectures, block copolymer self-assembly, star-shaped oligomers, hydrogen-bonding networks, polymer blends with locally high-concentration domains, and targeted grafting of ion-conducting segments. The mechanisms by which these designs enhance Li + dissociation, migration pathways, and interfacial stability are critically examined, supported by quantitative performance metrics from recent literature. Finally, emerging trends such as multifunctional polymer frameworks, synergistic plasticization–reinforcement strategies, and interface-oriented molecular design are discussed, outlining a roadmap toward SICPEs with room temperature conductivities exceeding 10 − 3 S cm − 1 and sufficient modulus for effective dendrite suppression.

Sustainable approaches for MOF densification to enhance hydrogen storage
abstract: To enable large-scale use, hydrogen (H 2 ) requires improved storage solutions. Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) provide a promising physisorption-based approach to address the low volumetric density of H₂ at standard temperature and pressure (0.09 g/L), thereby significantly improving its viability as a clean energy vector. Although MOFs have a high surface area, their use in H 2 storage is still limited because of their low packing density. In this review, we critically assess densification strategies for enhancing volumetric H 2 storage, using representative case studies on HKUST-1, ZIF-8, MOF-5, UiO-66 and MIL-101(Cr). Notably, the HKUST-1 monolith demonstrated the highest total volumetric H 2 uptake (46.7 g/L) at 100 bar and 77 K, outperforming ZIF-8 (35 g/L), MOF-5 (43 g/L), UiO-66 co-pellet (+PAN; 32 g/L) and MIL-101 (Cr) (40 g/L) under the same conditions. These values show that densification bridges the gap between adsorption properties and practical H 2 storage requirements, though the industrial viability of HKUST-1 monolith remains subject to material cost and recyclability. A semi-quantitative sustainability assessment of all the densification methods is provided; it compares solvent intensity and energy use. Among these methods, dry extrusion, spray drying and sol-gel monolith route are the most readily adaptable to large-scale production and offer proven environmental benefits.

title: FeII based spin crossover Hofmann-type MOFs: Recent progress in spin state regulation, multifunctionality and applications
abstract: Hofmann-type metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), built from FeII centers, cyanometallate nodes and organic ligands, represent a prototypical class of porous coordination polymers. Their modular architecture allows precise tuning of dimensionality and ligand fields, enabling controllable spin crossover in response to temperature, pressure, light, or guest adsorption. This review first outlines recent advances in the synthesis of Hofmann-type MOFs across different material forms, from single crystals to thin films and nanoscale systems. The spin crossover behavior of both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) systems, is then examined, highlighting how cooperative elastic interactions, host-guest effects, weak intermolecular forces, and external stimuli govern transition profiles. Beyond magnetic properties, the integration of multifunctionality is discussed, where spin-state switching is coupled with optical, redox, dielectric, and electrical responses. Special attention is given to emerging applications in gas adsorption and separation, and catalysis. Finally, practical challenges related to structural stability, reversibility, and processability, are addressed and future directions are outlined for the rational design and scalable implementation of spin crossover-based frameworks as next-generation stimuli-responsive functional materials.

abstract: Two-dimensional transition-metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) have evolved from conductive layered solids into chemically programmable platforms for theranostics, wherein function is dictated by surface coordination rather than morphology alone. Their metal-rich basal planes and termination groups (–O, –OH, –F) establish dynamic coordination environments that govern ligand binding, redox activity, and interfacial charge transfer. This review positions coordination chemistry as the central framework linking MXene synthesis, defect structure, and surface functionalisation to biological performance. We examine how etching chemistry, oxidation state, and vacancy distributions define coordination sites that control drug adsorption pathways, binding strength, and stimulus-responsive release. Particular attention is given to interfacial complexes formed with polymers, metal ions, and biomolecules, which regulate colloidal stability, protein corona formation, pharmacokinetics, and immune interactions. The mechanistic origins of imaging contrast are analysed across modalities, including magnetic relaxation, X-ray attenuation, and photoacoustic response, with explicit correlations to metal identity, electronic structure, and ligand field effects. Recent advances in fluorine-free synthesis, Lewis acidic etching, and electrochemical routes are assessed in terms of their ability to produce stable, defect-controlled coordination landscapes. Strategies for oxidation control and surface passivation are evaluated against degradation kinetics and off-target reactivity in physiological environments. Emerging data-driven approaches for predicting coordination motifs and structure–property relationships are also discussed. By mapping coordination environments to measurable therapeutic and diagnostic outputs, this review defines design rules for MXene-based systems with controlled reactivity, predictable biological interactions, and improved translational viability in precision nanomedicine.

Host–guest supramolecular chemistry of carboranes: structural features and emerging applications in nanotechnology and nanomedicine
abstract: Carboranes are abiotic, polyhedral clusters containing boron, carbon and hydrogen atoms characterized by exceptional thermal and chemical stability, three-dimensional aromaticity, and unique electronic and structural features. Among them, carborane clusters containing two carbon atoms within the cage (dicarborane or C 2 -carboranes) represent a particularly important class, encompassing closo -dicarba-dodecaboranes, their nido derivatives, and related dicarbollide-based systems. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the interactions between dicarboranes and a wide range of hosts, including macrocycles, molecular cages, nanostructured materials, and biomolecules. The analysis highlights the diverse non-covalent interactions governing complex formation, such as hydrophobic effects, C-H···π and B-H···π contacts, dihydrogen bonding, and electrostatic contributions, which enable strong and tunable binding affinities. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationship between structural features, such as isomer type, cage topology, and functionalization, and host–guest behavior. We discuss how the rigidity, globular shape, and modular functionalization of dicarboranes contribute to enhanced host–guest recognition and facilitate the design of supramolecular assemblies with controlled size, morphology, and responsiveness. Emerging applications in nanotechnology and nanomedicine are highlighted, including self-assembled nanoplatforms, stimuli-responsive delivery systems, sensing, molecular machines, self-healing materials, and bioactive systems. In biomedical contexts, carborane-based systems have attracted considerable attention as pharmacophores, as well as in boron neutron capture therapy, bioorthogonal labeling, intracellular carrier and protein targeting strategies. Overall, the unique physicochemical properties of carboranes, combined with their versatile supramolecular behavior, position them as powerful building blocks for next-generation functional materials. This review highlights the growing importance of carborane-based host–guest chemistry, while delineating key limitations and future opportunities for its integration into advanced technological and biomedical applications.

Mechanochemistry for sustainable organometallic synthesis: A review across the d-block
abstract: Mechanochemistry has emerged as a powerful and increasingly mature approach for the synthesis of coordination and organometallic compounds, offering access to reaction pathways and products that differ fundamentally from those observed under conventional solution-based conditions. This review provides a critical overview of recent developments in the mechanochemical synthesis of d-block coordination complexes, with emphasis on studies published over the last decade and on contemporary contributions that reflect current advances in structural control, mechanistic understanding, and sustainability assessment. Focusing on molecular, structurally characterized species rather than extended frameworks, the review surveys mechanochemical reactivity across early-, middle-, and late-transition metals, highlighting how solvent-free or minimally solvated conditions influence metal-ligand interactions, coordination geometries and product selectivity. Particular attention is devoted to comparisons between mechanochemical and solution-based approaches, addressing when the two converge, and when mechanochemistry enables qualitatively different outcomes. Beyond synthetic efficiency, mechanochemical methodologies are analyzed through the combined lens of green chemistry metrics, reaction rates, yields, product distributions and apparatus-dependent effects. By integrating recent experimental advances with critical analysis, this contribution positions mechanochemistry as a complementary and conceptually distinct field within modern coordination and organometallic chemistry, rather than as a universal replacement for solution-based synthesis.

Relations between H–C and M–C bond strengths: influence of the organic ligand and the metal
abstract: This review describes the thermodynamics of C–H bond activation in various hydrocarbons, especially (poly)fluorinated benzenes, by transition metal complexes, through experiments and computational studies, with a focus on the latter. Experimental metal-carbon bond dissociation enthalpies (BDEs), determined relative to an internal reference, were used to establish the relationship between H–C and M–C BDEs. In parallel, bond dissociation enthalpies or energies were computed with DFT methods. For a given metal complex and a set of sufficiently similar organic substrates a linear correlation with a characteristic slope R M-C/H-C was obtained. Since far more H-C BDEs are known than M-C BDEs, these correlations provide a powerful predictive tool. Both experimental and computational studies indicate that the slope is always greater than 1 and quantitatively agree on its value when comparison could be made, suggesting a systematic thermodynamic preference for cleaving stronger hydrogen-carbon bonds. The R M-C/H-C value is particularly high for (poly)fluorobenzenes, with the greatest increase in M–C BDE occurring when fluorine atoms are ortho to the M–C bond, as found by experiments. Values of R M-C/H-C almost up to 3 have been reported. The polarity of the M–C bond, greater than that of the H–C bond, is suggested to be the cause of the high value of R M-C/H-C and the associated observed high selectivity in C–H bond activation. Recent experimental studies suggested that Co is more selective than Rh and Ir for C–H bond activation in (poly)fluorobenzenes. A computational study of the thermodynamics of C–H activation in C 6 F n H 6-n (n = 0, 5) by CpM(CO) (M = Co, Rh, Ir) confirms that R M-C/H-C is highest for Co and shows again a relation between R M-C/H-C and the polarity of the M–C bond. Additionally, the R M-C/H-C value is shown to be inversely related to the strength of the M–C bond since the Co–C BDE is the weakest for group 9 transition metals. Further studies are needed to confirm the generality of the finding that 3d transition metal complexes could be more selective in C–H activation than their heavier congeners. Correlations are also found between M–X and H–X (X = O, N) BDEs with slopes varying from 0.9 to 1.4. The ranking of M-X BDEs (M–C < M–N < M–O) is discussed as well as the magnitudes of the correlation slopes that is generally higher for aromatic substituents. Although this review is centred on reactions with thermodynamically controlled product distributions, some reactions are recognised in which kinetically controlled products follow thermodynamics. For all systems, computations appear to provide accurate information and can replace experiments if needed. Prediction of relative bond strengths in many organometallic species from knowledge of bond strengths for cognate organic molecules can be achieved.

abstract: Interest in the photophysics of low-spin, octahedral Fe(II) complexes of polypyridyl ligands has been sustained both by their intrinsically fascinating photodynamics, and the long-standing goal of replicating the photochemical properties of heavier metal photosensitizers in applications including photocatalysis and solar energy harvesting. A detailed understanding of the processes that follow photoexcitation has been, and will continue to be, critical for the field. This includes the energetic ordering and lifetimes of the various accessible excited states and the trajectory by which they decay, as well as an understanding of the structural dynamics involved in the relaxation mechanism. Here, we compile what is known about the excited-state landscape of [Fe(bpy) 3 ] 2+ (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridyl), reviewing the seminal contributions that have helped establish our current understanding of the photophysical processes that follow light absorption in this canonical 3d 6 metal coordination complex chromophore.

abstract: Intrinsic and extrinsic defect engineering strategies are the most ubiquitous zero-dimensional topological defects and prevalent in the transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) for hydrogen evolution. Such approaches tailor the crystal structure, phase, electronic states, electron transfer, and hydrogen adsorption energies (ΔG H⁎ ) of the TMDs. Defect-induced electronic redistribution and local lattice distortion create additional active sites and facilitate faster charge transfer, resulting in a reduction of overpotential, improved Tafel slope and optimum ΔG H⁎ . Here, we systematically summarize the intrinsic and extrinsic defect engineering strategies on TMDs that have been utilized to obtain an efficient hydrogen evolution reaction electrocatalyst. Contribution, such as vacancy, substitution, metal, nonmetal, and hybrid doping effects of TMDs towards hydrogen production, was concisely reviewed. In addition, the comparison of different TMDs along with their essential properties was displayed. Furthermore, representative case studies are presented to correlate defect structures with catalytic performance across different TMD systems. A comparative analysis of various TMDs and their essential properties is also provided. Finally, this review concludes with insights into future research directions for the development of advanced 2D TMD-based hydrogen production catalysts. This will bridge the existing knowledge gap by enhancing awareness of defect engineering among researchers currently working in this field.

Translating NIR-II imaging into clinical practice: advances and strategies
abstract: Near-infrared II (NIR-II) bioimaging has advanced rapidly through the development of diverse luminescent probes, improved detection hardware, and increasingly sophisticated imaging modalities. However, the translation of NIR-II imaging from preclinical demonstrations to practical biomedical use remains limited by a central challenge: probe performance, imaging-system configuration, computational processing, and application requirements are often optimized separately rather than as an integrated system. In this review, we discuss NIR-II bioimaging from a task-driven and system-level perspective. We first summarize the optical basis of NIR-II imaging and the evolution of major probe families, including single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), quantum dots (QDs), organic fluorophores, rare earth nanoparticles (RENPs), and metal nanoclusters. We then analyze how excitation sources, optical architectures, detectors, lifetime strategies, and computational reconstruction methods shape the effective performance of NIR-II imaging in vivo. Representative applications in tumor surgery, vascular and lymphatic imaging, brain imaging, and other disease models are further discussed according to their translational evidence levels. Building on these analyses, we propose a closed-loop framework in which clinical tasks define the required imaging window, probe properties, system architecture, quantitative readouts, and validation criteria. This framework emphasizes that future NIR-II bioimaging should move beyond isolated improvements in wavelength or brightness toward standardized, application-matched, and clinically realistic co-design of probes, instruments, algorithms, and biomedical workflows.

Properties and applications of porphyrin-based coordination polymers and networks
abstract: Coordination polymers (CPs) and networks represent a special class of materials exhibiting a wealth of quasi-custom-made properties opening the door to tailored applications. Using chromophore, emissive and electro-active ligands, the resulting coordination materials, either used as in its pristine form or as a composite possesses rich photophysical and redox properties, thus these features can be exploited advantageously. This is indeed the case for porphyrin-containing ligands, which are known to be both electro- and photochemically active. This article explores the structural traits of porphyrin-based-1D, 2D and 3D-CPs and networks, as well as their properties and applications, but excludes 3D-porous porphyrin-based metal-organic frameworks, PMOFs, which have been thoroughly reviewed in the past and nowadays. The covered properties are photophysics (including nonlinear optics and photosensitization), proton transport, magnetics, ferroelectric, and electric conductivity, and the applications includes electrochemical water splitting (including H 2 - and O 2 -evolution), CO 2 reduction, gas and molecule adsorption/trapping, antimicrobial, photodynamic therapy (PDT) and antimicrobial PDT (aPDT), catalysis, photocatalysis, sensors and solar cells.

Engineered nanoparticles for mitigating nervous system infections
abstract: Infections of the nervous system represent a heterogeneous and highly challenging disease category that includes both central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) infections. These infections mainly include meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria, toxoplasmosis, neurotuberculosis, viral-associated neurocognitive disorders, and PNS infections. Despite advances in antimicrobial therapies and supportive care, they remain among the leading causes of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. This review provides an in-depth overview of nanotechnology-assisted approaches to the treatment and diagnosis of CNS and PNS infections. We also discuss how diverse nanomaterials, including polymeric and lipid vesicles, as well as inorganic, biomimetic, catalytic, and stimuli-responsive materials, are engineered to overcome biological barriers, such as the blood-brain, blood-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood-nerve barriers, to target nervous system infections. Most importantly, nanomaterials are used not only to deliver therapeutics to target sites or improve diagnostics but also to interact with and manipulate biological processes to combat infections. The review also covers emerging trends in delivering nanomaterials to target nervous system infections, including intranasal delivery, biomimetic transcytosis, and pathogen-inspired mechanisms, as well as nano-assisted sensing approaches in CSF and peripheral biofluids. We further unify therapeutic and diagnostic approaches, highlighting nanotechnology's potential to address unmet medical needs.

Spectroscopic and computational mapping of excited-state dynamics: Lessons from Re(I) carbonyl complexes
abstract: The widespread application of Re(I) carbonyl complexes in photocatalysis, solar energy conversion, sensing, and imaging has driven efforts to understand their excited-state dynamics. Re(I) carbonyl complexes provide an ideal platform for illustrating excited-state mapping by spectroscopic and computational methods, as systematic ligand modification has produced a rich range of diimine and triimine systems with closely spaced electronic states and competing relaxation pathways. Recent advances in spectroscopic techniques have enabled mapping of the excited-state landscape across different time scales. The discussion is organized around the different stages of excited-state evolution. Resonance Raman (RR) spectroscopy is first used to probe the initially populated Franck–Condon states. Faster dynamics, analyzed by femtosecond transient methods, describe the evolution toward the thermally equilibrated excited state (THEXI), while slower dynamics and longer-lived states are examined using nanosecond transient methods. Vibrational spectroscopies, including transient infrared (TRIR) and transient Raman techniques, provide structural evidence for both short-lived intermediate states and the longer-lived THEXI state. As such, the techniques are discussed with emphasis on the information they provide and their limitations, and their application to Re(I) systems, where the electronic complexity increases from metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT)-dominated systems to systems with a complex interplay among MLCT, intraligand charge-transfer (ILCT), intraligand (IL), and mixed-character states. These examples highlight how solvent effects, charge-transfer character, and ligand-driven structural changes influence excited-state properties, switching, and lifetimes. In parallel, computational methods connect experimental spectra to electronic structure, excited-state energies, and orbital distributions. Recent developments in time-dependent Density functional theory (TDDFT)-based excited-state analysis, simulations of RR, TRIR, spectroelectrochemical, and transient absorption spectra, Marcus-type treatments of charge and energy transfer, and nonadiabatic wavepacket dynamics are also considered. Selected examples further extend these concepts to Re(I) probes in DNA and protein environments, illustrating how combined spectroscopic and computational approaches can reveal excited-state behavior in complex molecular and biological settings.

abstract: Photodynamic inactivation of microorganisms (PDI) is increasingly viewed not only as a light-triggered antimicrobial modality, but as a coordination chemistry-driven approach in which molecular structure, metal coordination, microbial targeting, excited-state dynamics, and irradiation conditions must be considered together. This Review examines tetrapyrrolic metal complexes and functional materials for PDI, with emphasis on heme-mimetic porphyrinoids, siderophore-guided delivery strategies, and hybrid photodynamic platforms. Rather than merely cataloguing photosensitizers according to structure, the discussion is organized around factors that determine biological performance, including interaction with microbial metal-acquisition pathways, bacterial uptake, metal-dependent photophysics, aggregation control, charge distribution, lipophilicity, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. A central theme is the distinction between receptor-mediated uptake and nonspecific membrane association. Heme-mimetic and siderophore-based approaches are evaluated as mechanistically distinct routes to bacterial targeting that impose different requirements on coordination geometry, ligand topology, and intracellular processing. Gallium porphyrinoids are discussed as iron-deceptive agents that combine heme-pathway recognition with disruption of iron-dependent metabolism, whereas zinc porphyrinoids are treated more cautiously as partial heme-like architectures whose activity often reflects membrane interactions, aggregation state, and favorable photophysics rather than experimentally validated active transport. The Review further examines how metal selection, molecular organization, functional materials, and adjuvant strategies influence photochemical pathways, ROS chemistry, and translational potential. We argue that clinically relevant antimicrobial PDT will depend less on identifying universally superior photosensitizers than on matching coordination design, formulation, light delivery, and material architecture to specific infection environments. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for the development and clinical translation of antimicrobial photodynamic systems.

abstract: Over the past decade, a rapidly expanding body of literature has reported structurally diverse silver(I) complexes incorporating a wide range of ligand classes, including N-, O-, S-, and P-donor systems, as well as biologically active scaffolds such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, amino acids, and antibiotics. However, despite the wealth of reported cytotoxicity data, direct comparison of biological performance remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of experimental conditions and the frequent absence of systematic selectivity evaluation. In this context, the present review provides a comprehensive and quantitative framework for analyzing the anticancer activity of silver(I) complexes, integrating normalized selectivity descriptors based on global z-score analysis of IC 50 values. This approach enables, for the first time, a statistically robust comparison across structurally diverse systems, facilitating the identification of structure-activity and, critically, structure-selectivity relationships that define the next generation of silver(I)-based anticancer agents.

title: Brain-inspired neuromorphic electronics of 2D materials: synapses to hardware systems
abstract: The rapid growth of data-intensive AI workloads has highlighted the energy and latency limits of the von-Neumann architecture, in which the physical separation of memory and processing drives the so-called memory wall. Brain-inspired neuromorphic electronics addresses this bottleneck by co-locating storage and computation in artificial synapses whose conductance encodes the synaptic weight. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), graphene, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), van der Waals (vdW) ferroelectrics, and layered chalcogen phosphates are widely explored as platforms for such synapses because of their atomic thickness, clean vdW interfaces, tunable defect/polarization landscapes, and compatibility with low-temperature hetero-integration. This review systematically explores the field along a single thread from synapses to hardware systems. We first summarize the neuromorphic computing paradigm and the neural network architectures (ANN, DNN, CNN, SNN) that have established the device-level requirements. We then discuss the key switching mechanisms in 2D synapses, including ion migration, charge trapping, ferroelectric polarization, phase/Mott transitions, and coupled photo-ionic/photo-ferroelectric effects and benchmark device performance against energy per event, ON/OFF ratio, endurance, retention, analog linearity, and variability. Particular attention is given to TMDC-based and TMDC-heterostructure synapses, which dominate recent demonstrations. Engineering strategies (wafer-scale growth, BEOL compatibility, reliability, sustainability) and the remaining challenges (variability, endurance, large-area uniformity, benchmarking beyond MNIST) are critically evaluated. We conclude with perspectives on adaptive robotics, secure on-device learning, and biohybrid interfaces, and outline a roadmap toward brain-scale, AI-grade 2D neuromorphic chips.

Advanced early diagnostics for infectious diseases through electrochemiluminescence
abstract: Rapid, sensitive and accessible diagnosis is central for improving the management of infectious diseases, particularly in vulnerable populations and settings where access to centralized testing is limited. Hence, this review examines recent advances in electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensing for early pathogen detection, with a focus on the coordination chemistry of typical luminophores, metal–based nanostructures and hybrid materials that underpin assay performance. Particular attention is devoted to transition-metal complexes, coordination polymers, supramolecular and porous hosts, and metal-organic and inorganic nanoplatforms capable of acting as ECL emitters, as well as on coreactant carriers and recognition scaffolds in immunoassays, aptamer– and oligonucleotide–based sensing, on imaging strategies and portable formats such as paper–based and microfluidic devices. Across representative examples targeting whole viruses and bacteria, pathogenic nucleic acids or clinically relevant biomarkers, these architectures have achieved high analytical sensitivity and, in several cases, are compatible with point-of-care implementation. Overall, the work critically discusses structure–property relationships governing ECL efficiency, signal amplification and assay robustness, and outlines design principles for next-generation ECL platforms aimed at bridging the gap between analytical performance and practical clinical implementation in both high- and low-resource healthcare contexts, supporting earlier diagnosis, improved treatment decisions, and broader infection surveillance.

abstract: The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) to methanol (CH 3 OH) offers a promising route for coupling carbon mitigation with renewable energy storage. Among molecular electrocatalysts, cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) and its derivatives have emerged as leading platforms owing to their well-defined Co N 4 coordination environment, tunable electronic structure, and adjustable intermediate-binding properties. Recent advances in ligand engineering, multinuclear architectures, catalyst–support interactions, and reaction microenvironment modulation have led to notable improvements in CH 3 OH selectivity and activity, with reported Faradaic efficiencies exceeding 30% and current densities above 100 mA cm −2 . However, achieving simultaneously high selectivity, activity, and durability remains challenging, and the mechanistic origins of CH 3 OH formation are not yet fully understood. In particular, the interplay among CO 2 activation, *CO stabilization, proton-coupled electron transfer kinetics, competitive CO desorption, and catalyst degradation continues to restrain rational catalyst design. This review summarizes recent advances in CoPc-based catalysts for electrochemical CO 2 -to-CH 3 OH conversion, with emphasis on reaction mechanisms, structure–reactivity relationships, degradation pathways, and molecular and interfacial engineering strategies. By integrating insights from operando spectroscopy, theoretical modeling, and membrane-electrode-assembly development, we highlight key design principles and identify remaining challenges toward the development of efficient, selective, and durable CoPc-based systems for practical CH 3 OH electrosynthesis.

Cross-disciplinary translation of paper-based sensors for bacterial detection
abstract: Rapid detection of pathogenic bacteria is needed for clinical diagnosis, food safety, and environmental monitoring. Culture, PCR, and ELISA remain reliable, but their use outside laboratories is limited by long turnaround times, instruments, trained personnel, and sample-processing requirements. Paper-based sensors address part of this gap because they are inexpensive, portable, disposable, and driven by capillary flow, while supporting colorimetric, fluorescent, electrochemical, chemiluminescent, and smartphone-based readouts. Recent work has combined paper-based devices with microfluidics, nanomaterials, molecular biology, materials chemistry, electronics, and data analysis. For coordination chemistry, the central question is how metal-ligand chemistry changes the performance of these devices. Metal complexes, metal nanoparticles, metal nanozymes, metal-organic frameworks, coordination polymers, and aggregation-induced emission materials can improve bacterial enrichment, probe immobilization, catalytic amplification, optical/electrochemical transduction, and interface stability. This review discusses paper-based bacterial sensors from this coordination-chemistry perspective, covering device construction, analytical methods, detection targets, artificial-intelligence-assisted readout, commercialization, and applications in environmental, food, and clinical samples. We also compare how coordination structures affect sensitivity, selectivity, matrix tolerance, cost, and translational potential. Finally, we discuss remaining barriers, including quantitative reliability, interference from complex samples, reagent storage, batch reproducibility, biofilm detection, standardization, and commercial implementation, and outline directions for practical coordination-material-enabled paper diagnostics.

abstract: The convergence of copper coordination chemistry and nanomedicine is catalyzing a transformative shift in metal-based therapeutics, addressing long-standing pharmacological barriers that have hindered clinical translation. Copper coordination compounds (CCCs) have long been recognized for their therapeutic potential, particularly in oncology, owing to their ability to generate reactive oxygen species and localize to mitochondria. However, their clinical application has been limited by poor aqueous solubility, systemic off-target toxicity, and rapid in vivo clearance. This review examines how the strategic integration of CCCs with diverse nanocarrier platforms overcomes these obstacles, unlocking unprecedented therapeutic potential. Surveying the past five years of literature, we demonstrate that nanoformulation dramatically enhances anticancer activity against treatment-resistant malignancies, through mechanisms ranging from immunogenic cell death to the recently elucidated cuproptosis pathway. The repurposed disulfiram‑copper complex serves as a paradigmatic case study, illustrating how nanoencapsulation transforms a poorly bioavailable agent into a potent therapeutic. Beyond oncology, we explore expanding applications of CCC nanomaterials as antimicrobial agents, wound-healing dressings, and advanced diagnostic tools. The studies discussed here are very recent and predominantly preclinical; nevertheless, we discuss their potential for clinical translation. This review provides a forward-looking perspective on critical challenges: long-term toxicity, large-scale manufacturability, translational hurdles, and the opportunities for these sophisticated hybrid materials to redefine precision medicine across multiple disease contexts.

abstract: Generating clean hydrogen fuel in quantities adequate to replace fossil fuels is an essential milestone in the pursuit of net-zero emissions. The growth of hydrogen production is significantly influenced by improvements in the stability, efficiency, and durability of water-splitting technologies. Nanoscale material platforms, engineered to enhance surface area and address complex surface chemistries, hold considerable promise for accelerating hydrogen generation in electrochemical and catalytic systems, thereby advancing energy storage and conversion. Nonetheless, with the advent of more advanced material architectures, identifying the most efficient designs for water splitting and hydrogen evolution remains a significant challenge. This article explores how size and morphology in carbon-based nanoarchitectures serve as crucial factors in the thoughtful design of materials for these applications. This study investigates the impact of structural dimensionality, ranging from zero-dimensional quantum dots to one-, two-, and three-dimensional frameworks, on catalytic activity and performance in water-splitting and hydrogen-evolution reactions (Scheme 1). We evaluate recent advancements in carbon-based metamaterials and hierarchical nanoarchitectures, focusing on their potential for sustainable hydrogen production and the challenges they pose. In conclusion, we present an overview of the latest advancements and potential prospects in the design of carbon nanoarchitecture, aimed at facilitating significant progress in clean hydrogen technologies.

Revisiting halogenated corrosion inhibitors: uncovering the hidden role of halogen bonding beyond resonance, inductive and polarizability effects
abstract: Halogenated organic compounds are widely recognized as potential aqueous-phase corrosion inhibitors; however, their inhibition potential has traditionally been described primarily in terms of resonance (+R), inductive (−I), and polarizability effects. This perspective overlooks a largely unexplored yet potentially critical interaction, halogen bonding (XB), which can play a crucial role in controlling metal corrosion inhibitor interactions. In this review, we revisit the adsorption behavior of halogen-substituted inhibitors and argue for the explicit incorporation of XB into the mechanistic framework of corrosion inhibition. This review provides a comprehensive mechanistic and conceptual assessment of the potential role of XB, with particular emphasis on the origin of σ-hole interactions, tunable strength, and strong directionality, which contribute significantly to corrosion protection. This review proposes that halogenated corrosion inhibitors may engage in XB not only directly with the electron-rich inner Helmholtz plane (IHP) but also indirectly via pre-adsorbed hydroxides, oxides, and counterions. Moreover, XB may contribute an additional energetic term to the overall adsorption energy (E ads ), which generally acts synergistically with coordination (chemisorption), van der Waals forces, electrostatic attraction, and π-interactions. The present discussion shows that while XB may not be entirely dominant in all cases, it can significantly influence adsorption through cooperative and additive effects, mainly by promoting surface alignment, stabilizing protective films, and encouraging lateral intermolecular interactions. Moreover, XB also contributes greatly to bridging chemical and physical adsorption, retro-donation processes, and strengthening bonding between metal and inhibitor molecules. The literature indicates that the inhibitory potential of halogenated inhibitors follows the order of polarizability and σ-hole strength. The critical literature analysis shows that the adsorption behavior of several classes of halogenated inhibitors, including aromatic, Schiff base, and heterocyclic compounds, can be better explained by incorporating the concept of XB, along with resonance, inductive, and polarizability effects.

abstract: To realize the full potential of the porphyrin macrocycle across the life and materials sciences requires tailoring of substituents for control of conjugation, electronic communication, metal coordination, oxidation-reduction processes, photochemistry, supramolecular assembly, and solubility. trans -AB-porphyrins afford compact architectures while retaining versatile bifunctionality. Seven distinct routes for macrocycle formation have been developed. The routes have relied on 73 β-unsubstituted dipyrromethane building blocks (and 65 aldehydes) to directly afford 178 porphyrins comprising 117 distinct A and B groups. The trans- AB-porphyrins upon macrocycle formation are obtained as the free base or the Zn(II), Ni(II), or Pd(II) chelate, whereas subsequent metal coordination has afforded the Cu(II), Mn(III), and Eu(III) chelates. Some A and B groups include organometallic moieties containing Fe(II) or Co(II), while others are aimed at imparting aqueous solubility and achieving bioconjugation. Subsequent modification of the A and B groups, and derivatization of other sites on the macrocycles, have been employed for elaboration of the trans -AB-porphyrins. The present review presents all examples of the formation of trans -AB-porphyrins since their origin (1998) through 2025, discusses animating design features, and delves into the synthesis of ten representative tailored trans -AB-porphyrins. Particular foci include the coordination properties displayed by 10 single-crystal structures, the vast number of metal-coordination complexes of 2-acylpyrroles, and facially encumbering groups including swallowtail (i.e., symmetrically branched alkyl) motifs. The collection of methods may enable consideration of new routes to tetrapyrrole macrocycles. Selected unattained objectives of porphyrin chemistry are highlighted.

abstract: Divalent f -block chemistry has undergone rapid expansion in recent years, driven by advances in the stabilization of low-valent lanthanide and actinide complexes. Although f -elements were historically accessed in the +3 or higher oxidation states, the isolation of +2 species has revealed unusual spectroscopic signatures, distinct bonding motifs, and multiple accessible electronic configurations that influence their chemical and physical properties. These developments have generated opportunities in areas including quantum information science, molecular magnetism, catalysis, and luminescence. Computational chemistry has played a pivotal role in interpreting the electronic structure and reactivity of these systems. However, accurately modeling divalent f -block complexes remains challenging because of strong electronic correlation, multiconfigurational character, and the presence of close-in-energy competing electronic states. As experimental capabilities and theoretical methodologies continue to advance, a comprehensive assessment of divalent chemistry is both timely and needed. In this Review, we integrate experimental and theoretical perspectives to provide a systematic analysis of divalent lanthanide and actinide complexes across the f -block series. We critically assess the role of ligands in determining competing ground-state configurations ( f n d 1 vs. f n+ 1 ) resulting in their distinct spectroscopic, magnetic, and bonding properties. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies for predictive modeling and rational design of low-valent f -block molecular systems, with potential applications ranging from dinitrogen reduction to quantum technologies.

abstract: Electrocatalytic splitting of hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) has emerged as a promising strategy for the simultaneous production of clean hydrogen and recovery of elemental sulfur, offering a thermodynamically advantageous alternative to water electrolysis while addressing the environmental and safety challenges posed by this toxic industrial byproduct. This critical review systematically examines the fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic principles governing direct and indirect electrochemical H 2 S conversion pathways, with particular emphasis on sulfide oxidation reaction (SOR) mechanisms at the anode and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode. Advances in electrocatalyst design including transition metal sulfides, selenides, phosphides, heterostructures, and bifunctional architectures are evaluated alongside anti-passivation strategies, electrolyte systems (aqueous alkaline/acidic, ionic liquids, and non-aqueous), membrane technologies, and diverse cell configurations. Despite significant progress in activity and stability under idealized conditions, critical gaps persist in long-term durability against sulfur passivation, selectivity control, scalability under realistic industrial feeds, and integration into practical systems. By highlighting these limitations and proposing future directions in computationally guided catalyst discovery, operando characterization, and reactor engineering, this review aims to accelerate the transition of H 2 S electrolysis toward industrial viability.

title: Antioxidant nanozymes for regenerative medicine: mechanisms, design, and applications in tissue repair
abstract: Natural antioxidant enzymes play a central role in regulating oxidative stress within living organisms. During tissue repair following injury, these enzymes act synergistically to scavenge excess reactive oxygen species and maintain cellular redox homeostasis, thereby supporting cell proliferation and differentiation, resolving inflammation, and facilitating extracellular matrix remodeling. Inspired by the catalytic properties and regulatory mechanisms of natural antioxidant enzyme systems, antioxidant nanozymes are artificial catalytic nanomaterials that mimic the activity of natural antioxidant enzymes and have emerged as a promising platform to overcome the limitations of natural enzymes and promote tissue regeneration. This review systematically summarizes the classification and catalytic mechanisms of antioxidant nanozymes, along with mechanism-guided design strategies. We further highlight recent advances in their application in regenerative medicine, including skin wound healing, cardiovascular repair, cartilage regeneration, neural tissue repair, bone tissue regeneration, and ocular repair. Finally, the challenges and future prospects of antioxidant nanozymes in regenerative medicine are discussed.

Aluminium based hydrotalcite like compounds for direct lithium extraction: A critical review on crystallography and structure selectivity design
abstract: The accelerating demand for lithium is intensifying interest in direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies that minimise the environmental footprint of conventional solar evaporation ponds. Among sorbent-based DLE concepts, aluminium based hydrotalcite like compounds (Al-HTlc), particularly lithium aluminium layered double hydroxide (LiAl-LDH), are considered the most mature sorbent options, offering facile lithium (Li + ) recovery and high selectivity in highly saline chloride based solutions. Both properties arise from a distinct intercalation mechanism wherein Li + and its counter-anions (e.g. Cl − or SO 4 2− ) are co-intercalated into the crystal structure upon brine exposure. Li + selectivity arises partly from a steric match between Li + (ionic radius ∼ 0.76 Å) and the ∼0.7–0.8 Å octahedral vacancies of Al(OH) 3 -derived layers. Intercalation of competing divalent ions (e.g. Mg 2+ ) can be disfavoured by their substantially more negative hydration energies (−1830 vs −475 kJ mol −1 for Mg 2+ and Li + , respectively), which hinder the necessary dehydration. Here, we present a crystallography-focused critical review that links water–ion interactions and dehydration barriers, crystal layer and interlayer structure, and sorption kinetics to explain performance trends and derive practical design principles. Controlled comparisons show sorption capacity rising with brine concentration, potentially attributable to partial dehydration of Li + , Li Cl ion-pair co-intercalation, or both at elevated ionic strength. We identify the main development barriers: sulfate poisoning, excessive Li + desorption, and underutilised theoretical capacity; and evaluate defect engineering strategies including anion regulation, ion doping, stacking faults, and polymer intercalation, along with processing strategies, e.g. anion exchange, to address these gaps.

Advances in metal selenite nonlinear optical materials: halogens directed structure modulation and property optimization
abstract: Nonlinear optical (NLO) materials are essential for laser frequency conversion and wavelength extension. Metal selenites have emerged as a research hotspot due to their structural diversity, stereochemically active lone pairs, and wide transparency range. Early reported selenites largely concentrated on pure oxides, and the regulation of parameters like the second-harmonic generation (SHG) intensity depended on metal cations. The most commonly used cations are d 0 transition metals, because they favor the enhancement of SHG efficiency, but their d configurations often reduce the band gap of the material. In recent years, halogen ions have been introduced into selenite system to develop new NLO materials with superior comprehensive performance. Utilizing the differences in electronegativity, coordination ability, and other properties between halogen and oxygen ions, heteroleptic polyhedra can be constructed to increase the distortion of the anionic groups, thus enhancing the NLO response and making possible the design and synthesis of new functional motifs. In addition, halide ions possess gradiently varying electronegativity and deformability. These differences may lead to enhanced polarizability and gradually reduced band gaps in compounds with substitution from F to I. Up to now (May 22, 2026), no review has yet systematically addressed the effects of halogen ions on NLO properties of metal selenites. This article reviews the research progress on halogen-containing selenite NLO materials, which are divided into two main classes: selenite halides (without Se-X bonds) and halogenated selenites (with Se-X bonds). Selenite halides can be further categorized into single-metal, bimetal, and trimetal selenite fluorides, chlorides and bromides. The halogenated selenites NLO materials reported to date include only chlorinated selenites. This review systematically delineates the underlying mechanisms of halogen-mediated modulation of the SHG response and optical band gap, and provides a comprehensive discussion of the synergistic interplay between metal-oxyhalide polyhedra and selenite groups, thus unveiling the microscopic origins of the SHG enhancement and band-gap widening. It is hoped that these findings can provide theoretical guidance for the rational design of emerging selenite NLO materials.

title: Photoinduced mixed-valence systems based on MLCT excited states in bimetallic complexes
abstract: Among the different products of charge separation in the photosynthetic reaction center, symmetry-breaking and non-symmetry-breaking charge separated species have been identified. However, photosynthetic reaction-center models have mainly focused on the former. Non-symmetry-breaking charge separated products involve an oxidized special pair and a reduced redox-active fragment that is external to the special pair. Photoinduced mixed-valence systems based on metal-to-ligand charge transfer excited states in bimetallic coordination complexes are excellent models thereof. Their systematic study allowed to derive structure-property correlations, and to understand the effects of the transiently reduced ligand (called charge-transfer counterpart) on the properties of the bimetallic mixed-valence core. In this review, bimetallic photoinduced mixed-valence systems are analyzed in detail, focusing on their differences with their corresponding bimetallic ground-state mixed-valence systems, which lack the charge-transfer counterpart. Electronic and redox effects are discussed in terms of their physical origin, globally analyzing recent examples from the literature. These effects modulate critical properties of bimetallic mixed-valence systems, like metal-metal electronic coupling and charge-density distribution between the redox-active metal centers, all of which have a profound impact on excited-state lifetimes and reactivity. Therefore, they are important in the design of solar-energy conversion schemes which exploit bimetallic complexes to mimic the photosynthetic reaction center and generate solar fuels.
