Theoretical determination of anisotropic interactions and their modulation by the electric field
abstract: Understanding the origin and control of magnetic anisotropy in transition-metal complexes is a central issue in molecular magnetism, with direct implications for spintronics and quantum information science. This review presents a theoretical framework for the determination of anisotropic magnetic interactions from first principles, with particular emphasis on their microscopic origin and their modulation by external electric fields. We first outline the methodologies that enable the extraction of effective spin Hamiltonians from ab initio calculations, including the treatment of electron correlation and spin–orbit coupling within both first- and second-order regimes. Special attention is devoted to the derivation of physically meaningful isotropic and anisotropic parameters—such as magnetic exchange, zero-field splitting, Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions, and symmetric anisotropic exchange tensors—through effective Hamiltonian theory. The microscopic mechanisms governing these interactions are then analyzed for mono- and polynuclear complexes, highlighting the roles of ligand-field effects, covalence, orbital hybridization, and molecular symmetry. Through selected examples, we illustrate how these factors control both the magnitude and the nature of anisotropic interactions, and how they can be rationalized using quantum chemical wave functions and low-energy electronic spectra. Finally, we discuss the emerging possibility of tuning magnetic interactions via external electric fields. We show how electric fields influence charge distribution, geometry, and exchange pathways, leading to measurable variations in both isotropic and anisotropic magnetic parameters. These results underline the potential of electric-field control as a strategy for achieving magnetoelectric coupling at the molecular scale. Overall, this review highlights how ab initio approaches provide not only quantitative predictions of magnetic properties but also a detailed microscopic understanding, paving the way toward the rational design of molecular systems with controllable and tunable magnetic behavior.

title: Confining copper (I) iodide (CuI) modules in metal organic frameworks (MOFs): Structures and applications of CuI-MOFs
abstract: Bulk Copper(I) iodide (CuI) has been extensively investigated due to its interesting properties and promising applications in photodetectors, piezoelectrics, and transparent transistors. it forms multiple structural phases ( α , β and γ ), each exhibiting distinct structure-dependent properties, for example, the α - and β -CuI phases act as superionic conductors, whereas γ- CuI functions as a transparent p -channel transistor in p - n hetero/homojunction optoelectronic devices. Consequently, developing hybrid materials incorporating functional {Cu x I y } modules with diverse structures is highly desirable. Coordination assembly, enabled by the formation of coordinate bonds between CuI and organic ligands, has proven to be an efficient strategy for synthesizing Cu x I y ( L ) z hybrids (L = N-, S-, or P-based organic ligand). Further structural tunability can be achieved by constructing {Cu x I y } modules within metal organic frameworks (MOFs), where various coordination modes between metal centers and organic linkers enable a broader range of architectures. Tailoring bulk CuI into discrete {Cu x I y } motifs and periodically assembling them into ordered MOF frameworks under confined environments can lead to CuI-MOFs with enhanced structure-dependent properties distinct from those of pristine CuI. This review summarizes recent advances in CuI-MOFs, emphasizing the structural characteristics of {Cu x I y } modules confined within MOFs and their associated applications. Our aim is to highlight a powerful approach for designing functionally tailored materials, featuring unique structures and customizable properties through the integration of functional inorganic modules into MOFs. For clarity, this review excludes Cu x I y ( L ) z compounds constructed solely from {Cu x I y } modules and organic ligands.

High-entropy alloys as emerging electrocatalysts for seawater electrolysis
abstract: Direct seawater electrolysis could enable green hydrogen production without competing for scarce freshwater resources, but its practical use is limited by chloride oxidation, catalyst corrosion, scaling, impurity deposition and long-term electrolyser instability. High-entropy alloys and related high-entropy-derived catalysts provide a versatile platform for addressing these coupled challenges because their multimetallic active sites, lattice distortion, defect-rich surfaces and adaptive reconstruction can be tuned to regulate hydrogen and oxygen evolution while limiting chlorine evolution and chloride-driven degradation. This Review examines recent progress in high-entropy alloy, oxide, hydroxide, phosphide, sulfide and related electrocatalysts for seawater splitting, with emphasis on activity-selectivity-stability relationships rather than activity alone. We discuss how composition, surface reconstruction, defect chemistry, electronic modulation and electrolyte engineering influence HER and OER kinetics, chlorine suppression and corrosion resistance in model saline electrolytes and real seawater. We also highlight the need for realistic benchmarking, including high-current operation, long-term durability, direct chlorine/hypochlorite quantification, operando identification of reconstructed active phases, and scalable synthesis. The Review concludes by outlining how mechanistically informed catalyst design, robust electrolyser architectures and standardised seawater testing can move high-entropy electrocatalysts closer to practical hydrogen production.
